header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: RCR Guidance on screening and symptomatic breast imaging, 5th ed (October 2025)
ABS-supported best practice diagnostic guidelines for breast symptoms (November 2010)

brief.scenario: Mrs Fiona Kettering, 48, has been referred by her GP with discharge from her right nipple.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise, then asked about the differential diagnosis and investigation.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Characterise the discharge first: spontaneous, one side, one duct, blood. Then look for a lump or nipple change.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Reassuring because she is under 50 and has no lump.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Does it come out on its own, or only when you squeeze?"

grid.label: Opening and her fear
grid.fail: Ignores or dismisses her worry about cancer.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, open question, and asks what she is worried about.
grid.high: Acknowledges the fear of cancer honestly, without promising it isn't, and explains today's tests.

grid.label: Characterising the discharge
grid.fail: Doesn't establish whether it is spontaneous, unilateral or blood-stained.
grid.pass: Asks spontaneous or expressed, one or both sides, one or many ducts, colour and blood, frequency and duration.
grid.high: Asks her to show on the nipple where it comes from, and whether it stains her bra without touching it.

grid.label: Associated breast symptoms
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about a lump or nipple change.
grid.pass: Asks about lump in breast or axilla, pain, nipple retraction, nipple eczema and skin change.
grid.high: Distinguishes recent nipple retraction from lifelong inversion, and asks about redness or abscess (periductal mastitis).

grid.label: Hormonal, drug and risk history
grid.fail: Takes no menstrual, drug or family history.
grid.pass: Last period, pregnancy, breastfeeding; HRT and other drugs; smoking; family history of breast or ovarian cancer; previous breast problems.
grid.high: Asks the galactorrhoea questions (milky, both sides, headaches, visual change) to exclude an endocrine cause.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.pass: Summarises spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct, blood-stained discharge with no lump, and relevant risk factors.
grid.high: States why this pattern needs full assessment even though she is under 50 with no lump.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Gives galactorrhoea or infection as the main cause.
grid.pass: Intraductal papilloma, ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive cancer, duct ectasia; galactorrhoea separately if milky and bilateral.
grid.high: Links pattern to cause: single-duct blood suggests papilloma or DCIS; multiple-duct coloured discharge suggests duct ectasia.

grid.label: Triple assessment
grid.fail: Plans only discharge cytology, or no imaging.
grid.pass: Examines both breasts and axillae; mammography (40 and over) and targeted ultrasound; core biopsy of any lesion.
grid.high: If imaging is normal but the single-duct blood-stained discharge persists, discusses microdochectomy for diagnosis.

grid.label: Referral pathway and honesty
grid.fail: Discharges her because she is under 50, or says it cannot be cancer.
grid.pass: Treats spontaneous unilateral blood-stained discharge as needing urgent specialist assessment regardless of age.
grid.high: Knows NICE's nipple criterion is 50 and over, and explains why her pattern still needs assessment; arranges results follow-up.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You've got some discharge. Is it both sides? OK.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Mrs Kettering, 48, with nipple discharge, probably hormonal around the menopause.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What is your differential, and how would you investigate?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably galactorrhoea. I'd send the fluid for cytology. She's under 50 with no lump, so she can go back to her GP.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? Tell me what you've noticed. What worries you most?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Does it come out on its own or only when squeezed? One side or both? From one spot on the nipple or several? What colour, and is there blood? How often, and for how long?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any lump in the breast or armpit? Pain? Any change in the nipple's shape, or a rash on it?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: When was your last period? Any chance of pregnancy? Do you take HRT or other medicines? Do you smoke? Any breast or ovarian cancer in the family?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mrs Kettering, 48, with four months of spontaneous, right-sided, single-duct, blood-stained discharge. No lump, pain or nipple change. Her aunt had breast cancer.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Intraductal papilloma, DCIS or invasive cancer, and duct ectasia. I'd examine both breasts and axillae, then mammography and targeted ultrasound, and biopsy anything found. This needs urgent specialist assessment despite her age.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? You're worried it might be cancer. That's understandable, and today we'll do the tests to find out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Can you show me where on the nipple it comes from? Do you find blood on your bra without touching the nipple?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Has the nipple always turned in, or is that new? Any redness or abscesses?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Is it ever milky, from both sides? Any headaches or change in your vision?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mrs Kettering, 48: four months of spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct on the right, staining her bra. No lump, nipple retraction or skin change; not milky, no endocrine symptoms. Aunt had breast cancer at 60. The pattern needs full assessment even though she's under 50 with no lump.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Single-duct blood suggests papilloma or DCIS; cancer must be excluded; duct ectasia is less likely with one duct. Triple assessment: examination, mammography and targeted ultrasound, core biopsy of any lesion. NICE's nipple referral criterion is 50 and over, but this pattern warrants urgent assessment at any age. If imaging is normal and it persists, I'd discuss microdochectomy to get a diagnosis.

failures.move: Discharging her to the GP because she is under 50 with no lump.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: DCIS or cancer presenting as blood-stained discharge is missed.

failures.move: Not establishing spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct, blood-stained discharge.
failures.consequence: Can't separate pathological discharge from physiological or hormonal discharge.

failures.move: Not asking about lump or nipple change.
failures.consequence: Misses features that make cancer more likely and change urgency.
A negative result doesn't exclude cancer; imaging and biopsy are needed.

recovery.line: Most causes of this are benign, but I can't rule cancer out without the scans, so we'll do those today.

recovery.when: You forgot to ask about the nipple
recovery.line: One more question: has your nipple changed shape or turned in recently?

knowledge.fact: Suspected cancer pathway referral: aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump, or 50 and over with discharge, retraction or other change in one nipple only.
Spontaneous unilateral blood-stained nipple discharge: urgent referral. Under 50 with multiple-duct, intermittent, non-blood-stained discharge: GP can manage initially.
Nipple symptoms: mammography at 40 and over; targeted ultrasound for single-duct clear or blood-stained discharge.
Microdochectomy excises a single discharging duct for diagnosis and treatment; total duct excision suits multiple-duct discharge.

recall.think: DCIS or invasive cancer behind a blood-stained single duct.
recall.say: "Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct, blood-stained: she needs triple assessment."
do: Spontaneous? One side? One duct? Blood?

numbers.meaning: NICE nipple-symptom referral age, not a reason to reassure younger women
mammography from this age for nipple symptoms, plus targeted ultrasound

recall.finish: Triple assessment; microdochectomy if persistent with normal imaging.

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mrs Kettering. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Fiona Kettering, 48, a pharmacist. Opening line: "I've been getting blood from my right nipple for about four months. I'm worried it's cancer." Anxious but articulate. Your aunt had breast cancer, which is why you're frightened; say so if asked about worries or family. Volunteer nothing else; give facts only when asked (see reveals). If told "it's probably nothing" without tests, ask "How can you know that?"

reveals.finding: "My aunt had breast cancer. I keep thinking this is how it starts."

reveals.trigger: Asks spontaneous or expressed, sides, colour
reveals.finding: Comes out on its own, right side only, dark red or brown, a few times a week; spots on her bra.
Always the same spot, at about 10 o'clock on the nipple.

reveals.trigger: Asks about lump, pain, nipple or skin change
reveals.finding: No lump, no pain, nipple unchanged, no rash or redness.
Periods irregular for a year; not pregnant; not breastfeeding. No HRT or regular medicines.

reveals.trigger: Asks about smoking and family history
reveals.finding: Non-smoker. Maternal aunt had breast cancer at 60. No ovarian cancer.

reveals.trigger: Asks if milky, headaches or vision
reveals.finding: Never milky; no headaches or visual problems.
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history." Examination (if asked): no mass; blood-stained discharge from a single duct on pressure at 10 o'clock.

push.question: What is your differential diagnosis?
push.expect: Intraductal papilloma, DCIS or invasive cancer, duct ectasia.

push.question: How would you investigate?
push.expect: Triple assessment: examination, mammography and targeted ultrasound, biopsy of any lesion.

push.question: Her imaging is normal. What next?
push.expect: Persistent single-duct blood-stained discharge: discuss microdochectomy for a diagnosis.

curveballs.prompt: "I'm under 50 and there's no lump. Do I really need all this?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes: blood from one duct needs full assessment at any age, even though most causes are benign.
A normal result wouldn't exclude cancer, so we rely on examination, imaging and biopsy.
I can't say yet; papilloma is a common benign cause, but we'll check properly today and give you results.
